arml-2018-power-02a.title: An injection
arml-2018-power-02a.body:
Given a binary partition of $n$, insert a $1$ immediately after its last nonzero part (making it an $(n+1)$-tuple; the zeros shift right). The result is non-increasing, has parts in $\{0\}\cup\{2^k\}$, and sums to $n+1$, so it is a binary partition of $n+1$. E.g. $(2,2,1,1,0,0)\mapsto(2,2,1,1,1,0,0)$.

Different partitions of $n$ give different images (delete the inserted 1 to recover the original). So this map is injective and $p_2(n)\le p_2(n+1)$. ∎

arml-2018-power-02b.title: Odd numbers need a 1
arml-2018-power-02b.body:
**No.** Let $n$ be even. Every binary partition of the odd number $n+1$ contains a part $1$ (otherwise all parts are even and the sum is even). Deleting one $1$ gives a binary partition of $n$, and this is the inverse of the map "insert a 1 after the last nonzero part". So that map is a bijection and $p_2(n+1)=p_2(n)$ for every even $n$ — there are arbitrarily large $n$ with equality.

(For odd $n$ the inequality is strict: $n+1$ even also has the all-even partitions, which are not images of the map.) ∎

arml-2018-power-03a.title: Two classes
arml-2018-power-03a.body:
Let $n$ be even. A binary partition of $n$ either has all parts even, or has a part $1$.

**All parts even.** At most $\frac n2$ parts are nonzero (each is $\ge2$). Dividing every part by 2 and dropping the last $\frac n2$ entries (all zero) gives a binary partition of $\frac n2$; conversely, doubling the parts of a binary partition of $\frac n2$ and appending $\frac n2$ zeros gives an all-even binary partition of $n$. These are inverse bijections, so there are $p_2(\frac n2)$ such partitions.

**Some part equals 1.** The 1s are the only odd parts, and the sum $n$ is even, so there are at least two 1s. Deleting two 1s gives a binary partition of $n-2$ (as an $(n-2)$-tuple: remove two entries); conversely, inserting two 1s right after the last nonzero part of a binary partition of $n-2$ gives a binary partition of $n$ with at least two 1s. These are inverse bijections, so there are $p_2(n-2)$ such partitions.

Adding, $p_2(n)=p_2(\frac n2)+p_2(n-2)$. ∎

arml-2018-power-03b.title: Strong induction
arml-2018-power-03b.body:
**No such $n$ exists.** We show $p_2(n)$ is even for all $n\ge2$ by strong induction. $p_2(2)=2$ and $p_2(3)=2$.

- If $n>2$ is odd, $p_2(n)=p_2(n-1)$ (every partition of an odd number has a 1; removing one 1 is a bijection to partitions of $n-1$), and $n-1\ge2$, so it is even.
- If $n\ge4$ is even, $p_2(n)=p_2(\frac n2)+p_2(n-2)$ with $\frac n2\ge2$ and $n-2\ge2$, so both terms are even by induction.

Hence $p_2(n)$ is even for every $n>1$. ∎

arml-2018-power-04a.title: A single chain
arml-2018-power-04a.body:
The binary partitions of 5 are $1^5$, $21^3$, $2^21$, $41$ (padded with zeros). Each is obtained from the next by one split:
$$(1,1,1,1,1)\prec(2,1,1,1,0)\prec(2,2,1,0,0)\prec(4,1,0,0,0)$$
($41\to2^21$ splits the 4; $2^21\to21^3$ splits a 2; $21^3\to1^5$ splits the 2). By transitivity any two of the four partitions are comparable, so the set is totally ordered. ∎

arml-2018-power-04b.title: Splits can't create larger parts or remove 1s
arml-2018-power-04b.body:
Take $q=(4,1,1,1,1,0,0,0)$ and $q'=(2,2,2,2,0,0,0,0)$.

- $q\not\prec q'$: splitting never creates a part larger than the largest existing part; $q'$ has largest part 2, so a 4 can never appear.
- $q'\not\prec q$: splitting never removes a part 1 (it only splits parts $\ge2$), so everything below $q$ has at least four 1s, while $q'$ has none.

So $q$ and $q'$ are incomparable. (Other examples: $41^4$ and $2^31^2$; $421^2$ and $2^4$.) ∎

arml-2018-power-05a.title: Split everything
arml-2018-power-05a.body:
Let $p=(1,1,\dots,1)$. Given any other binary partition $p'$, it has a part $2^k$ with $k\ge1$; split it. Repeat. Each split increases the number of nonzero parts, which is at most $n$, so the process stops, and it can only stop when every nonzero part is 1 — i.e. at $(1,\dots,1)$ (the sum is still $n$). Hence $p\prec p'$ for every $p'\ne p$.

(Conversely nothing lies below $p$: it has no part that can be split.) ∎

arml-2018-power-05b.title: Merge equal parts
arml-2018-power-05b.body:
The inverse of a split is a *merge*: replace two equal nonzero parts $2^{k-1},2^{k-1}$ by one part $2^k$ (and add a 0). $P'\prec P$ means $P$ is reached from $P'$ by merges.

Start from any binary partition $P'$ and merge two equal nonzero parts as long as possible. Each merge decreases the number of nonzero parts, so this ends, at a partition with **distinct** nonzero powers of 2 summing to $n$. By uniqueness of binary representation this is $P=(2^a,2^b,2^c,\dots,0,\dots,0)$ where $n=2^a+2^b+2^c+\cdots$, $a>b>c>\cdots$.

So every binary partition $P'\ne P$ satisfies $P'\prec P$, and $P$ is the largest. ∎

arml-2018-power-06a.title: Vertices and edges
arml-2018-power-06a.body:
*Covers.* Each splitting step increases the number of nonzero parts by exactly one. Hence $q$ covers $p$ exactly when $p$ is obtained from $q$ by a **single** split.

The ten binary partitions of 8 by level (Level $=8-$ number of nonzero parts):

| Level | Vertices |
|---|---|
| 7 | $8$ |
| 6 | $4^2$ |
| 5 | $42^2$ |
| 4 | $2^4$, $421^2$ |
| 3 | $2^31^2$, $41^4$ |
| 2 | $2^21^4$ |
| 1 | $21^6$ |
| 0 | $1^8$ |

Edges (single splits): $1^8$–$21^6$, $21^6$–$2^21^4$, $2^21^4$–$2^31^2$, $2^21^4$–$41^4$, $2^31^2$–$2^4$, $2^31^2$–$421^2$, $41^4$–$421^2$, $2^4$–$42^2$, $421^2$–$42^2$, $42^2$–$4^2$, $4^2$–$8$.

So the diagram is a single path at the bottom ($1^8,21^6,2^21^4$), then a hexagon-like part: $2^21^4$ branches to $2^31^2$ and $41^4$; $2^31^2$ joins both $2^4$ and $421^2$, $41^4$ joins $421^2$; $2^4$ and $421^2$ both lead to $42^2$; then $4^2$ and $8$ on top.

arml-2018-power-06b.title: Follow the edges
arml-2018-power-06b.body:
The edges of the diagram are the single splits: $1^8$–$21^6$–$2^21^4$, $2^21^4$–$2^31^2$, $2^21^4$–$41^4$, $2^31^2$–$2^4$, $2^31^2$–$421^2$, $41^4$–$421^2$, $2^4$–$42^2$, $421^2$–$42^2$, $42^2$–$4^2$–$8$.

A Hamiltonian path:
$$1^8,\ 21^6,\ 2^21^4,\ 41^4,\ 421^2,\ 2^31^2,\ 2^4,\ 42^2,\ 4^2,\ 8.$$
Each consecutive pair is an edge and all 10 vertices appear once. (Starting at $1^8$ the path is in fact forced: $41^4$ must come right after $2^21^4$, since otherwise $41^4$ could only be entered from $421^2$ and would be a second dead end besides $8$.)

arml-2018-power-06c.title: Halve or remove two 1s
arml-2018-power-06c.body:
Define $B(p)$: if all parts of $p$ are even, halve every part (and drop the trailing $\frac n2$ zeros) to get an element of $S_1$; otherwise $p$ has at least two 1s (its sum is even), and $B(p)$ deletes two 1s, giving an element of $S_2$. As in the proof of $p_2(n)=p_2(\frac n2)+p_2(n-2)$, both pieces are bijections (inverse maps: double and pad with zeros; insert two 1s), and since $n>4$ we have $n-2>\frac n2$, so $S_1\cap S_2=\emptyset$ and $B:S\to S_1\cup S_2$ is a bijection.

**Order.** Suppose $p\prec p'$, so $p$ comes from $p'$ by a chain of splits $p'=q_0,q_1,\dots,q_m=p$. Splits never destroy a part 1, so the number of 1s never decreases along the chain.

- *$p'$ has 1s.* Then every $q_i$ has at least two 1s. Each split acts on a part $\ge2$, so deleting two 1s from every $q_i$ gives a valid chain of splits from $B(p')$ to $B(p)$: $B(p)\prec B(p')$.
- *$p$ has no 1s.* Then no $q_i$ has 1s, so every split replaces $2^k$ ($k\ge2$) by two $2^{k-1}$; halving every $q_i$ turns it into the split of $2^{k-1}$ into two $2^{k-2}$. So $B(p)\prec B(p')$ in $S_1$.
- *$p'$ has no 1s but $p$ has 1s.* Then $B(p')\in S_1$ and $B(p)\in S_2$ are partitions of different numbers, hence incomparable.

(The remaining case, $p'$ with 1s and $p$ without, is impossible.) ∎

arml-2018-power-06d.title: Strong induction with a prescribed endpoint
arml-2018-power-06d.body:
*Covers.* Each splitting step increases the number of nonzero parts by exactly one. Hence $q$ covers $p$ exactly when $p$ is obtained from $q$ by a **single** split.

**Odd $n$.** Every binary partition of odd $n$ contains a 1; deleting one 1 is a bijection to partitions of $n-1$ that maps single splits to single splits and back. So the Hasse diagram for $n$ is isomorphic to the one for $n-1$ (with $1^n\leftrightarrow1^{n-1}$), and it suffices to treat even $n$ (and $n=1$, a single vertex).

**Claim.** For even $n=a\cdot2^k$ ($a$ odd, $k\ge1$) there is a Hamiltonian path from $1^n$ to $(2^k)^a$ ($a$ parts equal to $2^k$).

*Base cases:* $n=2$: $1^2,2$. $n=4$: $1^4,21^2,2^2,4$.

*Inductive step* ($n=2r\ge6$). Split the vertices into $A$ = partitions with at least two 1s and $B$ = partitions with no 1s. Adding two 1s identifies the diagram of $n-2$ with the part of the diagram on $A$ (single splits correspond), and doubling identifies the diagram of $r$ with the part on $B$.

Write $n-2=c\cdot2^\ell$ with $c$ odd. By induction there is a Hamiltonian path of $n-2$ from $1^{n-2}$ to $(2^\ell)^c$; adding two 1s gives a path through all of $A$ from $1^n$ to $(2^\ell)^c1^2$.

- *$r$ even.* Then $n-2=2(r-1)$ with $r-1$ odd, so $\ell=1$ and the $A$-path ends at $2^{r-1}1^2$. Step to $2^r$ (merge the two 1s — an edge). Write $r=a\cdot2^{k-1}$; by induction there is a Hamiltonian path of $r$ from $1^r$ to $(2^{k-1})^a$; doubling gives a path through all of $B$ from $2^r$ to $(2^k)^a$. Concatenate.
- *$r$ odd.* Then $n=2r$ has $k=1$, $a=r$, target $2^r$. Now $r-1=c\cdot2^{\ell-1}$ is even, so $\ell\ge2$. Step from $(2^\ell)^c1^2$ to $(2^\ell)^c2$ (an edge; this is in $B$). Partitions of odd $r$ correspond to partitions of $r-1$ plus a 1; by induction there is a Hamiltonian path of $r-1$ from $1^{r-1}$ to $(2^{\ell-1})^c$, hence a path of $r$ from $1^r$ to $(2^{\ell-1})^c1$, and doubling gives a path through $B$ from $2^r$ to $(2^\ell)^c2$. Traverse it backwards, from $(2^\ell)^c2$ to $2^r$, and concatenate.

In both cases we get a Hamiltonian path from $1^n$ (the Level-0 vertex) to $(2^k)^a$, completing the induction. ∎

arml-2018-power-07.title: Induction on the level
arml-2018-power-07.body:
A single split replaces one part by two, increasing the number of nonzero parts by exactly 1; so $y$ covers $x$ iff $x$ is obtained from $y$ by one split, and then $y$ has exactly one fewer nonzero part than $x$.

Level 0 is the least element $1^n$, which has $n=n-0$ nonzero parts. Moving up one level along a covering edge always decreases the number of nonzero parts by one, so by induction every element at Level $L$ has $n-L$ nonzero parts. Conversely, any partition with $n-L$ nonzero parts is joined to $1^n$ by a chain of $L$ single splits (split until all parts are 1), so it lies at Level $L$. Hence $f_L(n)$ equals the number of binary partitions of $n$ with $n-L$ nonzero parts. ∎

arml-2018-power-08a.title: Examples
arml-2018-power-08a.body:
Allowed s-parts are $0,1,3,7,\dots$; binary parts are $0,1,2,4,\dots$

- s-partition of 7: $(3,3,1,0,0,0,0)$ (others: $(7,0,\dots,0)$, $(3,1,1,1,1,0,0)$, $(1,\dots,1)$).
- Neither: $(6,1,0,0,0,0,0)$, since 6 is neither of the form $2^j$ nor $2^j-1$. (Others: $(5,2,0,\dots)$, $(3,2,2,0,\dots)$, $(3,2,1,1,0,\dots)$.)

arml-2018-power-08b.title: Subtract one from each part
arml-2018-power-08b.body:
Let $p$ be a binary partition of $n$ at Level $L$, so it has exactly $n-L$ nonzero parts. Subtract 1 from each nonzero part: each $2^j$ becomes $2^j-1$, and the total becomes $n-(n-L)=L$. This gives an s-partition $\phi(p)$ of $L$ (parts $1$ become $0$).

**Inverse.** Given an s-partition $s$ of $L$, it has $m\le L$ nonzero parts. Since $n\ge 2L$, $n-L\ge L\ge m$. Add 1 to each of the $m$ nonzero parts and also include $n-L-m$ parts equal to $1$ (i.e. $0+1$), then pad with zeros to length $n$. The result has exactly $n-L$ nonzero parts, each a power of 2, with sum $L+(n-L)=n$: a binary partition of $n$ at Level $L$.

These two maps are inverse to each other (subtracting 1 from each of the $n-L$ nonzero parts undoes the construction and vice versa). So $f_L(n)$ equals the number of s-partitions of $L$. ∎

arml-2018-power-09.title: List the seven partitions

arml-2018-power-10.title: The diagram for 18
arml-2018-power-10.body:
**$n=18$ works** (so do 19 and 20, whose diagrams are isomorphic to it by appending one or two 1s).

The 12 trinary partitions of 18 and the covering edges (single replacements) are:
$1^{18}$–$31^{15}$–$3^21^{12}$–$3^31^9$; $3^31^9$–$91^9$; $3^31^9$–$3^41^6$; $91^9$–$931^6$; $3^41^6$–$931^6$; $3^41^6$–$3^51^3$; $931^6$–$93^21^3$; $3^51^3$–$93^21^3$; $3^51^3$–$3^6$; $93^21^3$–$93^3$; $3^6$–$93^3$; $93^3$–$9^2$.

$1^{18}$ and $9^2$ each have only one edge, so a Hamiltonian path must start at one and end at the other; say it runs from $1^{18}$ to $9^2$. It begins $1^{18},31^{15},3^21^{12},3^31^9$, and must end $\dots,93^3,9^2$.

- If the next vertex is $3^41^6$, then $91^9$ (whose neighbors are $3^31^9$ and $931^6$) can only be entered from $931^6$ and then is a dead end — but the path must end at $9^2$. Contradiction.
- So the path goes $3^31^9,91^9,931^6$. Now $3^41^6$ still has unused neighbors $931^6,3^51^3$ only.
  - If next is $93^21^3$: then $3^41^6$ can only be reached via $3^51^3$ and would be a dead end (both its other neighbors used). Contradiction.
  - If next is $3^41^6$, then $3^51^3$. The remaining vertices are $93^21^3$, $3^6$, $93^3$, $9^2$. From $3^51^3$ go to $93^21^3$ or $3^6$; either way we must next go to $93^3$ (their only other neighbor), leaving the other of $93^21^3$, $3^6$ to be visited after $93^3$, which then cannot reach $9^2$. Contradiction.

So there is no Hamiltonian path for $n=18$. ∎

(For comparison, $n=3,6,9,12,15,21$ do have Hamiltonian paths, e.g. $1^{12},31^9,3^21^6,3^31^3,91^3,93,3^4$; a computer check confirms 18, 19, 20 are the only failures below 23.)
